raw_text:
### Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global health challenge, characterized by high morbidity, mortality, and frequent hospitalizations [1]. Despite robust guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), a substantial portion of patients continue to suffer from persistent symptoms and functional limitations [2]. Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) is a well-established device therapy for patients with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and prolonged QRS duration (typically $\ge 130$ ms). However, approximately 70% of heart failure patients present with a narrow QRS complex (<120 ms), rendering them ineligible for CRT [3,4]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) has emerged as an innovative device-based therapy designed to address this therapeutic gap in patients with symptomatic HF, a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) between 25% and 45%, and a narrow QRS duration [5].

### Mechanism of Action

Unlike pacemakers or defibrillators that trigger myocardial contraction, CCM delivers high-voltage, non-excitatory electrical signals during the absolute refractory period of the cardiac cycle [6]. The primary target of CCM is the enhancement of myocardial contractility without increasing myocardial oxygen consumption ($MVO_2$), a distinct advantage over traditional inotropic agents [7,8]. At the cellular level, CCM signals stimulate the sarcoplasmic reticulum, rapidly restoring intracellular calcium handling [9,10]. It upregulates the expression and phosphorylation of phospholamban and the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase 2a (SERCA2a), while normalizing the function of ryanodine receptors [11]. Over the long term, CCM induces reverse remodeling by shifting the expression of fetal gene programs back toward normal adult profiles [12,13]. These genetic and biochemical alterations lead to a reduction in left ventricular volumes and improved mechanical efficiency [14]. Additionally, CCM has been shown to improve coronary microvascular perfusion [15] and restore autonomic balance by decreasing sympathetic activity and increasing parasympathetic tone [16].

### Clinical Evidence and Efficacy

The clinical utility of CCM has been rigorously evaluated in several randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Early feasibility studies demonstrated the safety and hemodynamic benefits of the therapy [17,18]. The FIX-HF-5 trial, which randomized 328 patients with NYHA class III/IV heart failure and LVEF $\le 35\%$, did not meet its primary endpoint of anaerobic threshold oxygen consumption ($VO_2$) in the overall cohort, but a retrospective subgroup analysis revealed significant improvements in exercise capacity (peak $VO_2$) and Quality of Life (QoL) in patients with LVEF between 25% and 45% [4,19].

This finding was prospectively validated in the pivotal FIX-HF-5C trial [3]. In this study, 160 patients with LVEF of 25–45% and narrow QRS complexes were randomized to receive either GDMT alone or GDMT combined with CCM. The CCM group demonstrated a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in peak $VO_2$ and Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire (MLHFQ) scores [3]. Furthermore, a significant reduction in the composite endpoint of cardiovascular mortality and HF hospitalizations was observed [3,20].

Long-term observational and real-world registry data have corroborated these trial findings. Studies by Schau et al. [14] and Naegele et al. [21] reported sustained improvements in functional class and survival rates over multi-year follow-ups that exceeded predicted mortality scores. Meta-analyses of clinical trials have confirmed that CCM consistently improves peak $VO_2$, 6-minute walk distance (6MWD), and QoL scores across diverse cohorts [5,22].

### Patient Selection and Clinical Implementation

Current clinical guidelines have integrated CCM as a therapeutic option for selected HF populations. The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines acknowledge CCM for symptomatic patients with LVEF 25–45% and QRS <120 ms to improve exercise capacity and quality of life [23], while the AHA/ACC/HFSA guidelines recognize its role in reducing hospitalizations and improving functional status in this subpopulation [24].

The target patient profile includes individuals with NYHA class III or ambulatory class IV symptoms despite optimal GDMT, LVEF 25–45%, and narrow QRS duration [3]. Notably, CCM has also shown utility in patients with wide QRS complexes who are non-responders to CRT [25,26]. Emerging data indicate that CCM is safe and effective in patients with permanent atrial fibrillation [27], as well as those with non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy [28]. The safety profile of the modern Optimizer device is highly favorable, with low rates of lead dislodgement, infection, or proarrhythmic events [29]. Recent investigations are also exploring the applicability of CCM in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [30], suggesting its mechanisms of action could extend beyond systolic dysfunction.

### Conclusion

Cardiac contractility modulation represents a crucial advancement in device-based heart failure management. By targeting intracellular calcium dynamics and genetic expression without increasing oxygen demand, CCM offers a unique physiological advantage. For the large cohort of symptomatic heart failure patients with moderately reduced LVEF and narrow QRS complexes who have limited treatment options, CCM provides a safe and effective means to improve exercise tolerance, quality of life, and clinical outcomes.
